samples.text: Advanced capabilities must never be allowed to pose unacceptable risks to human lives, human rights, or democratic integrity. Effective governance must also address deep developmental asymmetries. We are not entering the AI era from the same starting point. Managing this revolution requires closing critical gaps in digital infrastructure, computing resources, and technical expertise so that developing countries are not left behind. We need AI systems that uplift the vulnerable, strengthen national resilience, promote gender equality, and foster human-centered partnerships, not exclusion and fragmentation. put a face to the tireless migrant workers and seafarers who keep the global community afloat. Millions of migrant workers leave their homes to search for a better life, contributing immeasurably to the sustainable development of countries of origin, transit and destination. They are committed to full human rights, and fundamental freedoms regardless of status and deserve steadfast protection from trafficking and exploitation along perilous migration routes. Among them, our seafarers form an indispensable lifeline of global commerce. Nearly 90% of world trade moves by sea, supported by close to 2 million seafarers, more than 25% of whom are Filipinos. They are essential workers, yet increasingly vulnerable to conflict and attacks at sea. Just recently, an incident in the Strait of Hormuz claimed the lives of Filipino seafarers and injured many others. Their tragedy reminds us that maritime security is human security. Put a face to our identities as an archipelagic and maritime nation, where open and secure seas are our lifeblood. For the Philippines, The safety of ships and seafarers cannot be separated from supply chains and global commerce. Open and secure seas, free from interference and coercion, are vital to our security, our economy, and our people. International law must remain our guiding lighthouse, with UNCLOS, the Convention on the Law of the Sea, standing firmly as the constitution of the oceans. Next year marks the 45th anniversary of UNCLOS and the Manila Declaration on the Peaceful Settlement of International Disputes.

I am pleased to announce the Philippines' ratification of the BBNJ Agreement, and this is in line with our commitment to the rules-based international order and the 1982 UNCLOS. We are determined to advance the just governance of the oceans and the conservation of maritime biodiversity. In our reflection on evolving multilateralism to be more fit for purpose, we must consider progress in the way we account for our stewardship of resources. Our economic models must account for the health of our planet. We must measure our success in promoting development in larger freedom in our accountability to every nation and every person of the community. Societies thrive in diversity and inclusion. Ladies and gentlemen, we stand in the midst of a global revolution of people, of economies, and of technologies. Migration straddles these changes. The movement of people across borders sustains growth in countries of origin, transit, and destination alike. Every day, Filipino migrants across the world are a testament to this. They support health systems, advance education, and boost creative economies. The 1.9 million seafarers are the backbone of maritime trade that accounts for 90% of global commerce. The International Conference of Seafarers, Human Rights, Safety and Wellbeing held in Manila earlier this month affirmed that states and stakeholders are ready to do more for them. As migrants link our nations, their rights and dignity should be a gathering point, not a fault line for governments. Technology is the other defining force of our age, a connector, an enabler, an equalizer. Artificial intelligence offers promise, but carries profound risks. We must help build digital societies that bridges development divides rather than widen them, conforming with safeguards against misuse. Over the last 80 years, the United Nations Charter has served as a wellspring of purpose and action for those who rise equal to the task of delivering its promise. There is no alternative to the United Nations. There is no good global order other than one based on international law and the principle of the sovereign equality of states. A rules-based order is indispensable.

And on this point, Allow me to be optimistic. The BBNJ agreements enter into force this year after almost 20 years of negotiations. Almost 20 years. Measured against a political cycle, this is close to an eternity. Measured against the building of international law, it is sometimes the time needed to reach a compromise strong enough to last. The agreement proves that even today, we continue to build international law rather than dismantle it. And Belgium has invested greatly in this process. It helped launch the Blue Leaders, a coalition of countries working to protect at least 30% of the ocean by 2030 and secure an ambitious ICS treaty. The BBNJ agreements now gives us an essential tool to advance towards that protection goal. But 20 years of negotiations must not be followed by years of waiting. It is in that spirit that Belgium is offering to host the treaty's future secretariat in Brussels. We are ready to enable it to work from day one. It will be able to draw on our scientific expertise and on a community that brings together international organizations, embassies, and civil society. So that we have agreed together becomes real protection at sea. Beneath those same oceans run other vital routes. The cables that connect the continents and carry much of our digital communications and energy. Here too, our interdependence is plain to see. A break, an act of sabotage, or an attack can have consequences thousands of kilometers away. Protecting those connections is essential. But our responsibility in the digital world doesn't end with infrastructure. Artificial intelligence already confronts us with another question. How can we make full use of the possibilities created by innovation without allowing technology to move faster than our ability to protect people? I'm thinking in particular of children who are growing up in a world where AI can open extraordinary possibilities but also creates new vulnerabilities. We must neither hold back innovation out of fear, nor assume that it will regulate itself. As AI sees in the digital world, freedom needs rules if it is to remain freedom.

Do not invent quotes, countries, numbers or mandates. Distinguish prepared text from delivered text, AI from generic digitalization, and uncertainty from No. Return the strict requested JSON. This is an automated review, never a claim of human verification. Read every representative and boundary passage. Propose analytical theme definitions grounded in these statements. Separate technical AI safety from military/security concerns when warranted. Include minority positions; do not force one theme per cluster or a predetermined number. Every theme needs exact source examples, inclusion/exclusion and boundary cases.
